question: Which bone forms the front boundary of the pelvic floor?
explanation: Great job! The pubic symphysis sits right at the front, marking the anterior boundary of the pelvis. You've got this! [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h1)

question: Why is the pelvic floor shaped like a hammock?

options.A: To store excess fat reserves in the lower pelvis
options.B: To completely block all pelvic openings at rest
options.C: To anchor the major bones of the lower limbs
options.D: To support abdominal organs against downward pressure

explanation: Spot on! Just like a hammock catches you when you sit, your pelvic floor muscles hold up organs like the bladder and uterus against gravity. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h1)

question: Which muscle group makes up the main bulk of the pelvic floor?
explanation: You nailed it! The levator ani is the star player here—it forms the major muscular sling of the pelvis. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h2)

question: What is the main job of the puborectalis muscle?

options.A: Regulates the flow of urine from the bladder
options.B: Pulls the pubic bone upward during heavy lifting
options.C: Rotates the thigh outward at the hip joint
options.D: Forms a sling to help maintain fecal continence

explanation: Well done! The puborectalis loops behind the rectum to create a sharp angle, helping you hold stool until you're ready to go. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h2)

question: Which ligaments help prevent the uterus from dropping by supporting the upper vagina and cervix?
explanation: Correct! Think of the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments as sturdy suspension ropes keeping everything securely in place upstairs. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h3)

question: What can happen if the pelvic ligaments and fascia become weak?

options.A: Blood flow to the lower limbs is cut off
options.B: The thigh bones become unstable in the socket
options.C: Pelvic organs can descend or prolapse

explanation: Spot on. Without strong support from ligaments and fascia, gravity pulls the pelvic organs downward. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h3)

question: What must the pelvic floor muscles do to allow someone to pass urine?
explanation: That's right! To pee freely, these muscles have to let go and relax so the path is open. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h4)

question: A patient leaks a little urine whenever she coughs or sneezes. Which pelvic floor function has failed here?

options.C: Core stabilization for the spinal column

explanation: You got it! This is called stress incontinence—when the pelvic floor isn't strong or fast enough to close the urethra against sudden pressure like a sneeze. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h4)

question: Which nerve supplies most of the feeling and movement to the pelvic floor?
explanation: Brilliant! The pudendal nerve is the main highway for signals traveling to and from the pelvic floor. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h5)

question: Which spinal nerve roots give rise to the nerves of the pelvic floor?
explanation: Correct! Remember 'S2, 3, 4 keeps the pelvic floor off the floor!' A handy little trick for your exams. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h5)

question: What do we call it when the bladder bulges into the front wall of the vagina because of weak support?
explanation: You're doing great! A cysto-cele happens when the tissue between the bladder and vagina stretches, letting the bladder push forward. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h6)

question: Which issue is most commonly linked to pelvic floor muscles that are too tight?
explanation: Spot on! Muscles that can't relax (hypertonic muscles) often lead to spasms, discomfort, and trouble emptying the bladder. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h6)

question: Which complaint from a patient is a classic warning sign of pelvic floor trouble?

options.A: Feeling of heaviness or a bulge in the vagina
options.B: Sharp pain radiating down the arms
options.C: Inability to move the shoulder joints
options.D: Sudden numbness in the lower legs

explanation: Correct! That feeling of heaviness or seeing a bulge is a major clue that pelvic organs are slipping down. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h7)

question: Why is it important to note if a patient frequently strains during bowel movements?

options.A: Constipation directly damages the pudendal nerve roots in the lower spine
options.B: Bowel movements have no connection to pelvic floor health
options.C: Chronic straining places continuous downward pressure and stretches pelvic muscles
options.D: Straining causes the kidneys to produce excess urine

explanation: You nailed it! Pushing too hard over time stretches out those supportive muscles and fascia, weakening the whole sling. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h7)

question: What is the most common exercise used to strengthen the pelvic floor without surgery?
explanation: Easy peasy! Kegels are the classic squeeze-and-release exercises that build great pelvic strength. [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h8)

question: Why should a nurse teach a patient NOT to squeeze their buttocks while doing Kegels?

options.A: To avoid raising the patient's blood pressure
options.B: To ensure the correct pelvic floor muscles are being isolated
options.C: To prevent cramping in the leg muscles
options.D: To keep the bladder from emptying too quickly

explanation: Brilliant! Squeezing the glutes or thighs cheats the exercise. We want the actual pelvic sling doing the heavy lifting! [learn more](GNS121_U5_T11#GNS121_U5_T11_h8)
